title: Using AI Tools Safely
summary: Get the benefits of chatbots and copilots without leaking data or trusting wrong answers.

lessons.title: What you type may not stay private
points: Text, files and screenshots you give an AI tool are sent to the provider. Depending on the tool and settings, they may be stored, reviewed or used to improve models.
Consumer accounts and enterprise accounts often have very different data protections.
Treat a public AI chatbot like a public website: don't paste anything you wouldn't post publicly.

lessons.title: Never paste these
points: Passwords, API keys, tokens or other secrets.
Customer or employee personal data, health or financial records.
Confidential source code, contracts, unreleased plans, or anything labelled Confidential, unless the tool is approved for it.
lessons.tip: Use your organisation's approved AI tools. Using unapproved tools for work is called 'shadow AI'.

lessons.title: AI can be confidently wrong
points: Large language models can 'hallucinate': produce fluent, convincing answers that are false, including fake citations and code that doesn't work.
Check facts, numbers, legal or medical statements and sources yourself before relying on them.
You are responsible for what you send, publish or deploy, even if an AI drafted it.

lessons.title: AI-written code and agents
points: Review AI-generated code like a stranger's pull request: check for security flaws, secrets and licence issues.
AI models can suggest packages that don't exist. Attackers can register those names and fill them with malware, so verify every dependency.
Give AI agents the least access they need, and require human approval for actions like sending, paying or deleting.

questions.q: Which of these is safe to paste into a public AI chatbot?
options: A request to explain what a firewall does
questions.why: General questions with no sensitive data are fine. Customer data, secrets and confidential plans should never go into unapproved tools.

questions.q: AI chatbots always provide accurate, verified information.
questions.why: Models can hallucinate: confident, fluent output that is wrong. Verify important facts and sources.

options: Using AI tools for work that your organisation hasn't approved
An AI that works at night
questions.why: Unapproved tools may store or reuse your data in ways your organisation can't control or audit.

questions.q: An AI assistant suggests installing a code package you've never heard of. What should you do?
options: Verify the package exists, is the intended one and is reputable before installing
Ask the AI if it's safe and trust the answer
questions.why: AI models sometimes invent package names. Attackers publish malware under those names, so always verify dependencies.

questions.q: If an AI drafted an email or report, you are no longer responsible for its accuracy.
questions.why: You remain accountable for anything you send or publish. Review AI output before using it.

questions.q: An AI agent can read your inbox and send email for you. What's the safest setup?
options: Least access needed, with your approval before it sends anything
questions.why: Limiting permissions and keeping a human in the loop for high-impact actions reduces damage if the agent is tricked or wrong.

questions.q: Data protections can differ between consumer and enterprise versions of the same AI tool.
questions.why: Enterprise plans often include contractual data protections and admin controls that free consumer accounts may not.

questions.q: An AI tool gives you a statistic with a citation for your report. What should you do?
options: Open the cited source and confirm it says that
questions.why: AI can fabricate or misquote sources. Always check the original before relying on it.

questions.q: What should you do with AI-generated code before merging it?
options: Merge it, AI code is always secure
Review and test it like any other code, including for security issues
questions.why: AI-written code can contain bugs, insecure patterns or secrets. Normal review and testing still apply.

questions.q: Removing names but leaving unique details (job title, location, dates) always makes data anonymous.
questions.why: Combinations of details can re-identify people. Follow your organisation's rules and use approved tools for any personal data.

sources.title: UK NCSC & partners – Guidelines for secure AI system development
